hangeulSection.tocDesc: Explore the Korean writing system step by step.
hangeulSection.introP1: Hangeul is the Korean writing system, created in 1443 by King Sejong the Great and a team of scholars. Before Hangeul, Koreans used Classical Chinese characters (Hanja), which took years to master and were accessible only to the elite.
hangeulSection.introP2: King Sejong believed that every person — regardless of their social class — deserved to be able to read and write. He designed Hangeul to be intuitive and easy to learn. Legend says "a wise man can learn it in a morning, a fool can learn it in ten days."
hangeulSection.introP3: The system was published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum ("The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People"). Today, Hangeul is celebrated every year on October 9th (Hangeul Day) and is widely regarded as one of the most logical and scientifically designed writing systems in the world.
hangeulSection.jamoP1: The genius of Hangeul lies in how its characters (called jamo) were designed. Each consonant shape represents the position of the mouth, tongue, or throat when making the sound.
hangeulSection.jamoConsonantP1: The basic consonant shapes are pictographic — they depict the speech organs in the act of producing the sound:
hangeulSection.jamoConsonantList: ㄱ (g): shape of the tongue touching the soft palate | ㄴ (n): shape of the tongue tip touching the alveolar ridge | ㅁ (m): shape of the lips closed | ㅅ (s): shape of a tooth | ㅇ (ng): shape of the throat (circle)
hangeulSection.jamoCosmologyP1: Vowels are built from just three fundamental strokes, each representing one of the three elements of Eastern cosmology:
hangeulSection.jamoCosmologyHeaven: Heaven — the round dot (·), representing the sky above
hangeulSection.jamoCosmologyEarth: Earth — the horizontal stroke (ㅡ), representing the flat ground
hangeulSection.jamoCosmologyHuman: Human — the vertical stroke (ㅣ), representing a person standing upright
hangeulSection.jamoVowelBuildP1: All vowels are combinations of these three elements. For example: ㅏ (a) = vertical stroke + dot to the right (person facing the sun). ㅓ (eo) = dot to the left + vertical stroke (person facing away from the sun).
hangeulSection.consonantsIntro: Korean has 19 consonants: 14 basic and 5 double (tense). Each basic consonant shape represents the position of your mouth when you make the sound.
hangeulSection.doubleConsonantsIntro: Double consonants are made by writing the basic form twice. They are pronounced with tighter throat muscles and no aspiration — a sharp, tense sound.
hangeulSection.vowelsIntro: Korean has 21 vowels: 10 basic and 11 compound. They are all built from the three cosmological elements (·, ㅡ, ㅣ).
hangeulSection.compoundVowelsIntro: Compound vowels combine two basic vowels into one. For example: ㅘ (wa) = ㅗ (o) + ㅏ (a).
hangeulSection.silentIeungRule: Vowels never stand alone in Korean. When a syllable starts with a vowel sound, you must add the silent consonant ㅇ (ieung) as a placeholder. For example, the sound "a" is written 아 (ㅇ + ㅏ), not just ㅏ by itself.
hangeulSection.syllablesIntro: Korean characters are grouped into syllable blocks. Each block represents one syllable and contains 2 to 3 characters arranged in a square:
hangeulSection.syllablesBlockExplanation: The position of the vowel determines the layout: vertical vowels (ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅣ) go to the right of the initial consonant, horizontal vowels (ㅗ, ㅜ, ㅡ) go below it.
